world.bio: Beekeeper outside Austin for sixteen years. I keep about forty hives on borrowed ranch land out past Dripping Springs and sell raw honey, comb and beeswax candles at the Sunset Valley and Mueller farmers markets. Used to be a long-haul trucker, quit after my knees and my marriage both gave out. Sing bass in the choir at Mt. Zion Baptist.
skills_assets: Forty Langstroth hives, around thirty strong this season
Extraction shed with a four-frame extractor and a heated uncapping knife
A 2006 F-250 with a flatbed and a bad set of front brakes
Two farmers market stalls, Saturdays and Sundays, with regular customers
Honey sold under the label 'Brannigan Bees', 220 jars a month in season
Wildflower, mesquite and sumac honey varieties with their own followers
Church choir contacts: about 60 families who buy candles at Christmas

projects.name: Fall requeening
projects.text: Replacing queens in twelve colonies that went weak over the summer. Ordered mated queens from a breeder in Georgia; they arrive in two weeks. The drought killed half the wildflowers this year so the colonies are light going into winter. I'm feeding sugar syrup, two quarts a hive a week.

projects.name: Christmas candle batch
projects.text: Pouring about 400 beeswax candles for the holiday market. Using old muffin tins and a double boiler in the shed. Not efficient but each batch sells out.

projects.name: Finding new yard
projects.text: If the ranch land sells, I need somewhere to put forty hives by spring. No idea where to look. Haven't told the customers yet.

notes.text: Dry again. Thirty days without rain. The sumac bloomed three weeks late and thin. I walked the yard at dawn and the bees looked like old men waiting for a bus: grumpy, slow, not going anywhere.

Harold, who owns the ranch, came by the shed. Said he's putting the property on the market, forty acres plus the house, by end of October. He said, 'Walt, I'm sorry, I know the bees are where they are.' I said sure. I didn't say anything else because I didn't trust my voice.
Choir rehearsal. We're doing 'Wade in the Water' for the fall program. Brother Otis says I'm flat on the low notes. I said I'm sixteen years of beekeeping flat. He laughed.
Truck brakes squealing again, every hill coming down 290. $380 for pads and rotors, I have it, but I'm putting it off for the Georgia queens, $27 each plus shipping. Priorities, I tell myself.
Saturday market: sold 62 jars. A woman asked if I'd be there next year. I said yes. Was that a lie? Don't know yet.
Called a few ranchers. One said he had space but a neighbour who sprays pesticide. Another doesn't want 'commercial' on his land. A third, just no. Beekeeping on borrowed land is borrowed time.
Feeding syrup in the heat, got stung through the glove on my left wrist. Swelled a bit. I've been stung maybe forty thousand times in my life and it still hurts. Small comfort.

Church lunch after service. Ms. Clara asked about candle orders, said she'd take thirty. That's a good start. Brother Otis said the church has an old half-acre behind the fellowship hall. Said he'd mention it to the pastor but I told him not to bother. He said he'd bother anyway.
Moved eight hives to a trial spot by the creek. Checked on them twice. The bees seemed fine. I wasn't fine. Watching them fly out in the morning like nothing was wrong.

messages.text: Harold: Walt, I got a call from the realtor. She wants to do photos on the 20th. Walt: The hives will be out front. Harold: Could you move a few? Walt: I can move the ones near the drive. Harold: Appreciate it.
Rae: Dad, are you eating? Walt: Honey and cornbread. Rae: That's not a meal. Walt: It's a bee meal. Rae: Come to Dallas for Thanksgiving. Walt: If the bees are settled.
Manager: Your spot is renewed through December. Walt: Thank you. Manager: Do you still do beeswax candles? Walt: Yes, from November. Manager: Good, we'll put you near the holiday tent.
Otis: Pastor says he'll think about the half-acre. Walt: Tell him there's no rush. Otis: There is a rush, I've seen your face. Walt: Don't tell people my face.
Luis: Any news on the land? Walt: Not yet. Luis: I've got a spot in Bastrop but it's thirty minutes farther. Walt: I'd drive it. Luis: Let's talk after your queens come.

calendar.event: Realtor photos at the ranch, 10:00; move front hives
Georgia queens arrive by mail, Dripping Springs post office

relations.about: Ranch owner, in his 70s, selling to move near his kids in Colorado. Friendly, a little guilty.
Choir mate and old friend, a retired mechanic, knows everyone at church.
Lives in Dallas, nurses a brain injury unit, wants him closer.

constraints: Hives must be within 45 minutes of Austin to keep both markets
Won't place colonies where there's pesticide spraying
Can't afford to rent land at commercial rates
Winter moves are risky; best done before November
sensitive: His knees are bad and he worries about lifting supers for another ten years
Money is thin: about $1,100 left after the queens
Has not told his daughter about the land risk

disclosure_policy.t0_public: Beekeeper and honey seller at two Austin farmers markets.
